content: G protein-coupled receptor 32 (GPR32), also referred to as the RvD1 receptor, is a human receptor that belongs to the rhodopsin-like subfamily of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). It was first identified in 1998 through molecular cloning and was classified as an orphan receptor. This means that while its amino acid sequence is similar to known receptors, no specific ligand or biological function was initially identified for it. The amino acid sequence of GPR32 shares 39% identity with Formyl peptide receptor 1 (a receptor for N-formylmethionine-leucyl-phenylalanine and related chemotactic factors) and 35% identity with Formyl peptide receptor 2 (a receptor for N-formyl peptides and certain lipoxins, which are specialized pro-resolving mediators involved in resolving inflammation). The GPR32 gene is located on chromosome 19, specifically in the q13.3 region. Notably, there are no mouse or other orthologs of GPR32. The GPR32 protein functions as a G protein-coupled receptor, although the specific G protein subtypes it activates have not yet been identified. It is expressed in various human cell types, including blood neutrophils, activated CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells, T helper 17 cells, tissue macrophages, small airway epithelial cells, and adipose tissue. When GPR32 is expressed in Chinese hamster ovary cells, it has been shown to inhibit the cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling pathway under both baseline and forskolin-stimulated conditions. This suggests that GPR32 belongs to the class of orphan GPCRs with constitutive signaling activity. At least six members of the D-series resolvins (RvDs)—specifically RvD1, RvD2, AT-RvD1, RvD3, AT-RvD3, and RvD5—activate their target cells through GPR32. This has led to the receptor being named the RvD1 receptor. Resolvin D-series molecules are part of a broader class of specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs), which are metabolites derived from the omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). These molecules play a critical role in resolving inflammation, inhibiting inflammatory responses, and promoting the healing of inflammatory lesions in both animals and humans. The conversion of DHA into RvDs and the subsequent activation of GPR32 by these molecules is thought to be one mechanism by which omega-3 fatty acids exert their anti-inflammatory effects and potentially mitigate various inflammation-related and other diseases.
